sentences.text: Sinosauropteryx was a small bipedal theropod characterized by short arms, large first fingers, and a long tail. The animal possessed over 50 extremely elongated caudal vertebrae, which constituted 60% of its total body length.

Most paleontologists interpret the preserved filaments on Sinosauropteryx as a primitive type of feather. The dinosaur was covered in a coat of simple, filament-like feathers that indicated a countershading body pattern and a banded tail.

Sinosauropteryx was the first non-avian dinosaur taxon discovered with evidence of feathers. The species name S. prima means "first," honoring its status as the first discovered non-avian feathered dinosaur species.
This genus was the first dinosaur genus discovered in the Jehol Biota of Liaoning Province.
In a 2002 presentation, Longrich suggested that the banding patterns on Sinosauropteryx specimens preserve remnants of the animal's actual colouration.
The genus Sinosauropteryx was described by Ji Q. and Ji S. in 1996.
The species was originally named Compsognathus prima before being reclassified as Sinosauropteryx prima, which remains the type species of the genus.

The first fossil specimen of Sinosauropteryx prima was uncovered in August 1996 by the fossil hunter Li Yumin. All known fossils of Sinosauropteryx were found in the Yixian Formation in the Beipiao and Lingyuan regions of Liaoning, China.

A second species, Sinosauropteryx lingyuanensis, was named and described by Rui Qiu and colleagues in 2025. The holotype of S. lingyuanensis is a near-complete skeleton of a potential juvenile that preserves traces of feather integument.

Well-preserved fossils of Sinosauropteryx provide evidence regarding its diet and reproduction. Fossil evidence from specimen NIGP 127587 shows that Sinosauropteryx ate small, fast-moving lizards like Dalinghosaurus.
Specimen NIGP 127587 contained several small eggs in its abdomen, providing evidence of reproduction in Sinosauropteryx. The eggs of Sinosauropteryx measured 36 mm in length and 26 mm in width.

Sinosauropteryx is classified within the family Compsognathidae, a group of small, long-tailed coelurosaurian theropods. Sinosauropteryx inhabited China during the Early Cretaceous and was likely a close relative of the genus Compsognathus.

While initially placed in the family Compsognathidae, later analyses placed Sinosauropteryx in its own family, Sinosauropterygidae. A 2024 study by Andrea Cau questioned the classification of Sinosauropteryx and related taxa, recovering them in a polytomy within basal Coelurosauria that excluded the genus Compsognathus.

Sinosauropteryx lived in northeastern China during the Early Cretaceous period. Sinosauropteryx lived approximately 120 million years ago during the Aptian stage of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Asia.
The fossil beds containing Sinosauropteryx are dated to between 124.6 and 122 million years ago.

The climate of Sinosauropteryx's habitat was temperate with distinct seasons, averaging about 10°C annually, which implies unusually cold winters for the Mesozoic era likely due to high latitude. The environment where Sinosauropteryx lived experienced periodic mortality events caused by volcanic eruptions, wildfires, and noxious gases.

Some researchers have debated whether these filamentous impressions represent collagen fibers instead of feathers. There is a debated alternative interpretation suggesting the filamentous impressions are collagen fibers rather than feathers, though this is not widely accepted.

Researchers initially debated whether the filamentous structures on Sinosauropteryx were modern feathers or something else, with some suggesting they were stiffening structures from a frill. Some researchers proposed that the filaments were collagen fibers forming a frill on the back and underside of the tail, similar to modern aquatic lizards.
Researchers suggest that thick filaments being bundles of thin filaments is a more plausible hypothesis than them being a variant of quilled plumaceous feathers with a morphology opposite to birds.
